analysis.one_liner: Reinstates lapsed Superfund taxes on oil and chemical companies to pay for toxic site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have restored expired taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic waste cleanups, died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action.
analysis.plain_summary: The "polluter pays" taxes that financed the Superfund program — which cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites — expired in 1995, shifting the cleanup bill to ordinary taxpayers. This bill would have brought those taxes back: an excise tax on petroleum and chemical feedstocks and a corporate environmental income tax, both running through 2013. The money would have replenished the federal trust fund that pays to clean contaminated sites. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream from Superfund toxic waste sites, whose cleanups would have been funded by the companies that created the pollution rather than by general tax revenues. Communities with abandoned contaminated land also benefit, since a funded Superfund program can more often hold polluters accountable and restore sites to usable condition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near toxic waste sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund excise tax on petroleum and chemical feedstocks through January 1, 2013, restoring a dedicated funding stream for toxic site cleanups.
Reinstates the Corporate Environmental Income Tax through January 1, 2013, so corporations again help finance cleanup of hazardous waste sites.
The bill's own text shows these taxes applied only through the end of 1995, meaning the polluter-funded portion of Superfund had lapsed; cleanup costs have been borne by general taxpayers instead.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and petroleum importers pay the per-barrel excise tax, and corporations with profits above a threshold pay the environmental income tax. Some of that cost would likely have been passed through to consumers in slightly higher prices for gasoline, motor oil, and products made from taxed chemicals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and chemical companies, partly consumers

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on crude oil and chemical feedstocks are typically passed through to consumers, so households would pay somewhat more for gasoline, motor oil, and chemical-based products.

An honest supporter must acknowledge that sites still get cleaned under the current system — just from general taxpayer revenues rather than a dedicated industry tax — so opponents can argue the bill raises prices without changing what gets cleaned, only who writes the check.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: a modest per-barrel tax and a corporate environmental tax, spread across oil and chemical companies, in exchange for a dedicated cleanup fund so taxpayers don't foot the entire bill for contamination those industries created. The pass-through to consumers is real but small relative to the cleanup burden that otherwise lands on general revenues. The main weakness is that the bill only raised money; it did not change cleanup standards or enforcement, so its value depended entirely on the funds actually being spent on cleanups.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on June 6, 2002, joined by original cosponsors including Republican Sen. Lincoln Chafee and Independent Sen. James Jeffords.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction.
Twenty senators cosponsored the bill: 18 of 49 Senate Democrats, 1 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Senate Independents.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further Senate action after the June 6 referral for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.
The bill would have restored the Superfund financing rate and the Corporate Environmental Income Tax, both of which the bill's text shows last applied before January 1, 1996.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, chemical, and other corporate polluters kept the benefit of the taxes that expired in 1995, while the cost of cleaning up toxic sites stayed with general taxpayers.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 18 of 49 Senate Democrats cosponsored versus 1 of 49 Republicans — and the bill never got to a floor vote where the split could have been tested.

industries.note: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products, a per-barrel charge the industry has not paid since 1995. Its interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the public's interest in having polluters, rather than taxpayers, fund cleanups.

The excise tax covers chemical feedstocks used in manufacturing, restoring a cost the industry avoided after the tax lapsed in 1995. The companies that generate hazardous waste would help pay to clean it up.
The Corporate Environmental Income Tax would have reapplied to corporate profits above a threshold, raising taxes on the largest companies through 2013.

With the polluter taxes lapsed, toxic site cleanups are financed from general revenues, meaning ordinary taxpayers have effectively picked up the bill since 1995. The bill would have shifted that burden back to industry, though some of the tax could have been passed through to consumer prices.
